processing: As with other Yunnan raw pu-erh, the leaf is typically wilted, wok-fired, rolled and sun-dried into mao cha, then sold loose or steamed and pressed; no ripe-style pile fermentation.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as is usual for Mengku raw pu-erh; little is documented about the season here beyond that.
appearance_dry: Little is documented; expect the long dark green strands typical of Yunnan large-leaf raw tea.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear golden yellow when young, as with other Yunnan raw tea.
appearance_wet: Typical of large-leaf raw tea: thick, olive-green leaves.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting record exists for this name, so any note is a guess. Expect the general strength and sweetness of Lincang raw pu-erh.

brewing.notes: General settings for strong young sheng, since nothing specific is recorded.

vintage_note: Listed in the trade with separate prices for old-tree and young-tree leaf, so ask which you are getting. Like other sheng it should be sold by harvest year, usually as spring tea. Little else is documented about how it reaches the market.
description:
Bakanan is a name from the Yunnan pu-erh trade, listed among the province's named mountain teas. Very little else is on record, including which hamlet exactly it refers to, and its filing under Mengku here is a working placement.

Nothing specific is documented about how it is made. It would be expected to follow the usual raw pu-erh method of Lincang, so treat the description of the cup as typical of that class only.

One published list of spring prices puts old-tree leaf at about two and a half times the price of young-tree leaf. That gap is the most useful thing a buyer can know: the label needs to say which one it is, and a seller should be able to name the village.
history: Little is documented. The name appears in a trade price list of Yunnan mountain teas, with no account of its growers, its age or how it became known.
